questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is poultry? Name any five types.
questions.a: Poultry are birds kept at home for meat, eggs and money. Any five of: chicken, turkeys, ducks, guinea fowls, geese, pigeons.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any six external parts of a domestic fowl.
questions.a: Any six of: comb, wattle, beak, eyes, feathers, wings, legs with scales, claws, tail, vent.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give three differences between a cock and a hen.
questions.a: A cock has a big comb and wattles, bright feathers, long pointed tail feathers and spurs, and it crows; a hen has a smaller comb, a rounded body, lays eggs and broods.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the four systems of keeping poultry and describe two.
questions.a: Free range, deep litter, battery cage and fold. (Describe two, for example: in deep litter birds are kept in a house on a floor covered with coffee husks or wood shavings; in free range the birds move about freely and look for their own food.)

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any three breeds of chicken and what each is kept for.
questions.a: Any three: White Leghorn — eggs; broilers — meat; Rhode Island Red — meat and eggs; local kienyeji — meat, eggs and hardiness.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any six ways of caring for poultry.
questions.a: Any six of: provide a clean, dry, well-ventilated house; give clean water always; feed a balanced ration; vaccinate; deworm and dust against parasites; isolate sick birds; remove wet litter; protect from predators and thieves; keep records.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any four poultry diseases and any three poultry parasites.
questions.a: Diseases: Newcastle, coccidiosis, fowl typhoid, fowl pox, gumboro (any four). Parasites: lice, mites, fleas, ticks, worms (any three).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the three types of bees in a colony and the work of each.
questions.a: Queen — the only fertile female, lays all the eggs; drones — males that mate with the queen; workers — sterile females that collect nectar, make honey, build combs, feed the young, guard and clean the hive.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give two traditional and two modern types of beehives.
questions.a: Traditional: log hives and pot or basket hives. Modern: the Kenya Top Bar hive and the Langstroth hive.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any four things to consider when siting an apiary.
questions.a: Any four of: a quiet, shady place; near water and flowering plants; away from homes, paths and animals; safe from thieves; protected from ants by greasing the wires.
accepted: protected from ants by greasing the wires

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give the steps followed when harvesting honey.
questions.a: Harvest in the evening or early morning → wear protective clothing → light the smoker and calm the bees → open the hive quietly → cut only combs with sealed honey, leaving some for the bees → put the combs in clean containers → close the hive → strain the honey and store it in a cool, dry place.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Why is protective clothing and a smoker used during harvesting?
questions.a: Because bees sting to defend the hive. Protective clothing keeps the stings off the body, and the smoke calms the bees so they do not attack the harvester.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any five products got from bees.
questions.a: Any five of: honey, beeswax, propolis, royal jelly, bee venom, and pollination services.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any five reasons why poultry and bee keeping are good businesses.
questions.a: Any five of: they need little land and little capital; they give food and income; they create employment; droppings give manure; bees pollinate crops; the products sell easily; they can be run beside other work.
accepted: they need little land and little capital
they can be run beside other work

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any four records a poultry farmer should keep.
questions.a: Any four of: numbers of birds bought and sold; eggs collected each day; feeds used and their cost; vaccinations and treatments given; deaths; income and expenses.
accepted: numbers of birds bought and sold

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give the difference between mass and weight.
questions.a: Mass is the amount of matter in an object and never changes; weight is the pull of gravity on the object and changes from place to place.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the instrument and the unit used for measuring: mass, weight, volume of a liquid.
questions.a: Mass — beam balance, in kilogrammes; weight — spring balance, in newtons; volume of a liquid — measuring cylinder or jug, in litres or millilitres.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give the difference between capacity and volume.
questions.a: Capacity is how much a container can hold; volume is the space a substance occupies.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Change: 3 kg to grammes; 2.5 litres to millilitres; 4,000 cm³ to litres.
questions.a: 3 kg = 3,000 g; 2.5 litres = 2,500 ml; 4,000 cm³ = 4 litres.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Find the volume of a box 8 cm long, 5 cm wide and 4 cm high.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Why are standard measures better than the hand span or the calabash?
questions.a: Because standard measures are the same everywhere and never change, while a hand span or calabash differs from person to person, so trade would be unfair and measurements could not be repeated.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What makes an object float or sink?
questions.a: An object floats if it is less dense than the liquid and sinks if it is more dense. Its shape also matters, because a shape that holds air pushes aside more water.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give three objects that float and three that sink in water.
questions.a: Float: wood, cork, a plastic bottle with air (also ice, oil). Sink: a stone, a nail, a metal spoon (also sand, glass).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Why does an iron sheet sink while a boat made of iron floats?
questions.a: The flat sheet is denser than water so it sinks; the boat shape holds air and pushes aside much more water, so the boat as a whole is less dense than water and floats.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Describe an experiment to show that an egg floats in salty water.
questions.a: Put an egg in a glass of fresh water — it sinks. Add salt slowly, stirring, and keep watching. As more salt dissolves, the water becomes denser, and at some point the egg rises and floats. This shows that a liquid's density affects floating.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Describe the displacement method for finding the volume of a stone.
questions.a: Pour water into a measuring cylinder and read the level. Lower the stone gently on a string until it is fully covered. Read the new level. Subtract the first reading from the second — the difference is the volume of the stone.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: A stone raises the water level in a cylinder from 30 cm³ to 75 cm³. Find its volume.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Define density and give its formula and unit.
questions.a: Density is the mass of a substance in a given volume. Density = mass ÷ volume, measured in g/cm³.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: An object of mass 240 g has a volume of 60 cm³. Find its density.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: A block of density 2.5 g/cm³ has a volume of 40 cm³. Find its mass.
questions.a: Mass = density × volume = 2.5 × 40 = 100 g

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is soil? Give the two ways in which it is formed.
questions.a: Soil is the loose top layer of the earth's surface in which plants grow. It is formed by the weathering of rocks and the decomposition of dead plant and animal matter.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name three kinds of weathering and give an example of each.
questions.a: Physical — heat and cold cracking rocks; chemical — water and chemicals dissolving rocks; biological — plant roots and burrowing animals breaking rocks.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the three types of soil and give two properties of each.
questions.a: Sandy — large particles, drains very fast, poor at holding water; clay — very small particles, sticky when wet and hard when dry, holds too much water; loam — a mixture with plenty of humus, holds enough water and drains well.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Which soil is best for farming, and why?
questions.a: Loam, because it holds enough water but still drains well, contains air and plenty of humus, and is easy to work.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Which soil is used for making pots and bricks, and why?
questions.a: Clay, because its very fine particles stick together when wet and become hard when dried or fired.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the layers of a soil profile from the top.
questions.a: Top soil → sub soil → weathered rock → bedrock.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the five components of soil.
questions.a: Mineral (rock) particles, air, water, humus and living things.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Describe an experiment to show that soil contains air.
questions.a: Drop dry soil into a container of water. Bubbles rise to the surface, showing that air was trapped in the spaces between the soil particles.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Describe an experiment to show that soil contains water.
questions.a: Put soil in a dry test tube and heat it gently. Drops of water appear on the cooler upper part of the tube, showing that the soil contained water.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Describe an experiment to show that soil contains humus.
questions.a: Heat soil strongly in a tin or on a metal sheet. It gives off smoke and a burning smell and becomes lighter in colour, showing that the humus has burnt away.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any six importances of soil.
questions.a: Any six of: it anchors plants and supplies water and mineral salts; it is used for farming; it is a home for soil animals; it is used for building bricks and roads; it is used for pottery; it holds and filters water; some soils contain minerals.
accepted: it anchors plants and supplies water and mineral salts
it is a home for soil animals
it is used for building bricks and roads

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is soil erosion? Name any four types.
questions.a: Soil erosion is the carrying away of the top soil by water, wind or animals. Types: sheet, rill, gully, wind erosion and landslides (any four).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any five causes of soil erosion.
questions.a: Any five of: cutting down trees; bush burning; overgrazing; farming on steep slopes; over-cultivation; poor road drainage; heavy rain falling on bare soil.
accepted: heavy rain falling on bare soil

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is soil exhaustion, and what causes it?
questions.a: Soil exhaustion is the loss of soil fertility. It is caused by growing the same crop again and again, over-cultivation, and failing to add manure or rest the land.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any eight methods of soil conservation.
questions.a: Any eight of: mulching; terracing; contour ploughing; strip cropping; crop rotation; applying manure and compost; planting cover crops and trees; controlled grazing; fallowing; digging trenches and check dams.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is immunity? Name its two types.
questions.a: Immunity is the ability of the body to fight and resist disease. Its two types are natural and acquired (artificial) immunity.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give three examples of natural immunity.
questions.a: Any three of: the skin, tears, saliva and stomach acid; white blood cells; antibodies a baby gets from the mother and from breast milk; immunity left after recovering from a disease.
accepted: antibodies a baby gets from the mother and from breast milk
immunity left after recovering from a disease

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is immunisation, and what is a vaccine?
questions.a: Immunisation is giving a person a vaccine so that the body can make antibodies and resist a disease. A vaccine is a medicine, usually made from weakened or killed germs, given to protect the body.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any six immunisable childhood diseases.
questions.a: Any six of: tuberculosis, polio, diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus, measles, hepatitis B, Haemophilus influenzae type b (also pneumonia and rotavirus today).
accepted: Haemophilus influenzae type b (also pneumonia and rotavirus today)

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Which vaccine protects against tuberculosis, and when is it given?
questions.a: BCG, given at birth, on the right upper arm.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Which five diseases are covered by the pentavalent vaccine?
questions.a: Diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus, hepatitis B and Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: At what ages are polio and pentavalent vaccines given?
questions.a: Polio at birth, 6, 10 and 14 weeks; pentavalent at 6, 10 and 14 weeks.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: At what age is the measles vaccine given?
questions.a: At 9 months (with a later second dose).
accepted: At 9 months (with a later second dose).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is the cold chain, and why is it necessary?
questions.a: The cold chain is the system of keeping vaccines cold from the factory to the child. It is necessary because vaccines are spoilt by heat and strong light and would then fail to protect the child.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any four ways of caring for vaccines.
questions.a: Any four of: keep them in a refrigerator or cold box with ice packs; carry them in a vaccine carrier; check the temperature with a thermometer; keep them out of sunlight; never use them after the expiry date or when the vial monitor shows they are spoilt.
accepted: carry them in a vaccine carrier
check the temperature with a thermometer
never use them after the expiry date
when the vial monitor shows they are spoilt

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is an immunisation card, and why must it be kept safely?
questions.a: It is the card that shows all the vaccines a child has received and the dates. It must be kept safely so that health workers know which doses are still due, and it is often needed when joining school.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any five importances of immunisation.
questions.a: Any five of: it prevents killer diseases and disabilities; it reduces child deaths; it is cheaper than treatment; it keeps children healthy and in school; it has wiped out smallpox; it protects the whole community.
accepted: it prevents killer diseases and disabilities
it keeps children healthy and in school

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Which disease has been wiped out completely by immunisation?
questions.a: Smallpox.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any five problems that hinder immunisation in Uganda.
questions.a: Any five of: ignorance and rumours; long distances and poor roads; power failure spoiling vaccines; parents forgetting or losing the card; insecurity in some areas; shortage of funds, staff or vaccines; religious or cultural objections.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Suggest a solution to each of: rumours about vaccines, long distance to the clinic, power failure, forgetting the appointment.
questions.a: Rumours — health education by radio, schools and village health teams; long distance — outreach and mobile clinics; power failure — solar fridges, cold boxes and ice packs; forgetting — reminders from village health teams and keeping the card where it is easily seen.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is digestion? What is the digestive system?
questions.a: Digestion is the breaking down of food into a form the body can absorb and use. The digestive system is the system of organs that breaks down food, absorbs it and removes the waste.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the parts of the alimentary canal in order.
questions.a: Mouth → oesophagus (gullet) → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum → anus.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give the work of: the mouth, the stomach, the small intestine, the large intestine.
questions.a: Mouth — chews the food and mixes it with saliva, which starts digesting starch; stomach — churns food with gastric juice and acid, which kill germs and start digesting protein; small intestine — completes digestion and absorbs the food into the blood; large intestine — absorbs water and mineral salts.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is peristalsis?
questions.a: Peristalsis is the squeezing, wave-like movement of the walls of the alimentary canal that pushes food along.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the four associated organs of the digestive system and the work of each.
questions.a: Salivary glands — produce saliva; liver — produces bile, stores food and removes poisons; gall bladder — stores bile; pancreas — produces pancreatic juice.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Which organ makes bile, where is it stored, and what does bile do?
questions.a: The liver makes bile; it is stored in the gall bladder; bile breaks fats into small drops so they can be digested easily.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the four types of teeth and the work of each.
questions.a: Incisors — cutting and biting; canines — tearing; premolars — crushing and grinding; molars — chewing and grinding.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: How many teeth has an adult, and how many has a child?
questions.a: An adult has 32; a child has 20 milk teeth.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Into what is each of these digested: starch, protein, fats?
questions.a: Starch → simple sugars (glucose); protein → amino acids; fats → fatty acids and glycerol.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Where does most absorption take place, and through what?
questions.a: In the small intestine, through tiny finger-like structures called villi.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any six diseases or disorders of the digestive system and give the cause of each.
questions.a: Any six, for example: diarrhoea — germs in dirty food and water; dysentery — bacteria or amoeba; cholera — bacteria in contaminated water; typhoid — bacteria in food and water; worms — worm eggs from dirt; constipation — little water and roughage; ulcers — too much acid and skipping meals; tooth decay — sugary foods and poor brushing.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give the signs of dysentery and of intestinal worms.
questions.a: Dysentery: stool with blood and mucus, stomach pain and fever. Worms: stomach pain, pot belly, loss of weight, tiredness and anaemia.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is ORS, and how is a home mixture prepared?
questions.a: ORS is oral rehydration salts, given to replace water and salts lost in diarrhoea. A home mixture: one litre of boiled, cooled water + eight level teaspoons of sugar + half a teaspoon of salt, stirred until dissolved.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any eight ways of keeping the digestive system healthy.
questions.a: Any eight of: eat a balanced diet with roughage; drink clean boiled water; wash hands with soap; wash fruits and cover food; chew well and eat at regular times; deworm every six months; brush teeth twice a day; use a clean latrine; avoid alcohol and self-medication; seek treatment early.
accepted: eat a balanced diet with roughage
chew well and eat at regular times

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Why should hands be washed with soap before eating?
questions.a: Because germs and worm eggs from dirt, faeces and animals stay on the fingers. When we eat with dirty hands they enter the mouth and cause diarrhoea, dysentery, typhoid, cholera and worms. Soap removes them.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is matter? Give its three properties.
questions.a: Matter is anything that has mass (weight) and occupies space. Properties: it has mass, it occupies space and it exerts pressure.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the three states of matter and give two examples of each.
questions.a: Solid — stone, ice; liquid — water, milk; gas — air, steam.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the change of state in each: ice to water; water to steam; steam to water; water to ice.
questions.a: Ice to water — melting; water to steam — evaporation (boiling); steam to water — condensation; water to ice — freezing.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Define solute, solvent and solution, with an example of each.
questions.a: Solute — the substance that dissolves, e.g. salt; solvent — the liquid it dissolves in, e.g. water; solution — the mixture formed, e.g. salty water.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give the difference between soluble and insoluble substances, with two examples of each.
questions.a: Soluble substances dissolve, for example salt and sugar; insoluble ones do not, for example sand and stones.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any six methods of separating mixtures and what each is used for.
questions.a: Any six: hand picking — large pieces; winnowing — light from heavy; sieving — small from large; filtering — solids from liquids; decanting — settled solids from a liquid; evaporation — a dissolved solid; distillation — a pure liquid; magnetic separation — magnetic materials.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: How would you separate: salt from salty water; iron filings from sand; chaff from millet; mud from water?
questions.a: Salt from salty water — evaporation; iron filings from sand — a magnet; chaff from millet — winnowing; mud from water — filtering (or decanting first).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is heat? Name any five sources of heat.
questions.a: Heat is a form of energy that makes things hot. Sources: the sun, fire from firewood or charcoal, electricity, friction, chemical reactions (also geothermal heat and the body).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the three ways in which heat travels and say where each mainly occurs.
questions.a: Conduction — mainly in solids; convection — in liquids and gases; radiation — through empty space, needing no material.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Describe an experiment to show conduction of heat.
questions.a: Take a metal rod and stick pins along it with wax. Heat one end in a flame. The wax melts and the pins fall one after another from the hot end outwards, showing that heat travelled along the solid by conduction.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Describe an experiment to show convection in water.
questions.a: Heat water gently in a clear glass container and drop in a coloured crystal (or sawdust). The colour rises from the heated part, spreads at the top, sinks at the sides and circles, showing convection currents.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any four good conductors and any four poor conductors of heat.
questions.a: Good conductors: copper, aluminium, iron, silver. Poor conductors: wood, plastic, rubber, glass (also dry cloth, air, paper).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Why are saucepans made of metal but their handles of wood or plastic?
questions.a: The metal body conducts heat quickly to the food so it cooks fast, while the wooden or plastic handle is a poor conductor, so it stays cool and the cook is not burnt.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any five effects of heat on matter.
questions.a: Any five of: expansion when heated and contraction when cooled; change of state; burning; drying; killing germs; cooking food.
accepted: expansion when heated and contraction when cooled

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any five uses and any four dangers of heat.
questions.a: Uses (any five): cooking; boiling water to kill germs; warming the body and house; drying clothes and food; ironing; welding; generating electricity; making bricks and pots. Dangers (any four): burns and scalds; fires; smoke causing chest disease; suffocation from a charcoal stove in a closed room.

topics.title: Occupations in Our Community — Crop Growing

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Occupations in Our Community — Crop Growing
questions.q: What is a tuber? Give the two types with two examples of each.
questions.a: A tuber is a swollen underground part of a plant in which food is stored. Root tubers — sweet potatoes and cassava; stem tubers — Irish potatoes and some yams.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Occupations in Our Community — Crop Growing
questions.q: How can you tell a stem tuber from a root tuber?
questions.a: A stem tuber has buds or "eyes" from which new shoots grow; a root tuber has no eyes and is grown from cuttings or the crown.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Occupations in Our Community — Crop Growing
questions.q: What planting material is used for: sweet potatoes, cassava, Irish potatoes, carrots?
questions.a: Sweet potatoes — vine cuttings; cassava — stem cuttings; Irish potatoes — seed tubers with eyes; carrots — seeds.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Occupations in Our Community — Crop Growing
questions.q: Give the steps followed in growing a tuber crop.
questions.a: Choose a suitable site → prepare the land into ridges or mounds → select clean planting materials → plant at the right spacing at the start of the rains → weed regularly → earth up → apply manure and rotate crops → control pests and diseases → harvest and store properly.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Occupations in Our Community — Crop Growing
questions.q: Why are tuber crops planted on ridges or mounds?
questions.a: Because ridges and mounds give loose, deep soil for the tubers to swell in, and they drain well so the tubers do not rot.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Occupations in Our Community — Crop Growing
questions.q: What is earthing up, and why is it done?
questions.a: Earthing up is heaping soil around the base of the plants. It covers the tubers so they do not become green or be attacked by weevils, supports the plant and controls weeds.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Occupations in Our Community — Crop Growing
questions.q: Name any five pests of tuber crops and the damage each causes.
questions.a: Any five: sweet potato weevil — bores into tubers, making them bitter; moles and rats — eat tubers underground; termites — eat stems and roots; aphids and whiteflies — suck sap and spread viruses; nematodes — cause galls and stunted plants.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Occupations in Our Community — Crop Growing
questions.q: Name any four diseases of tuber crops and their signs.
questions.a: Any four: cassava mosaic — yellow, twisted, small leaves; cassava brown streak — brown rot inside the tuber; potato blight — leaves turn black and the plant dies; bacterial wilt — sudden wilting and death.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Occupations in Our Community — Crop Growing
questions.q: Which insect spreads cassava mosaic?
questions.a: The whitefly.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Occupations in Our Community — Crop Growing
questions.q: Give any six ways of controlling pests and diseases of tuber crops.
questions.a: Any six of: plant clean, disease-free materials; use resistant varieties; practise crop rotation; earth up; weed and keep the garden clean; remove and burn diseased plants; harvest in time; trap rats and moles; use pesticides correctly; seek advice from the extension officer.
accepted: weed and keep the garden clean
seek advice from the extension officer

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Occupations in Our Community — Crop Growing
questions.q: Why should a farmer plant clean, disease-free cuttings?
questions.a: Because diseases such as cassava mosaic and brown streak are carried in the cuttings themselves. Planting infected material spreads the disease to the whole garden, however well the farmer weeds or sprays.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Occupations in Our Community — Crop Growing
questions.q: Give any four rules for harvesting tuber crops.
questions.a: Any four of: dig carefully with a hoe or fork so the tubers are not cut or bruised; harvest when mature; harvest sweet potatoes piecemeal as needed; lift Irish potatoes when the leaves turn yellow; avoid harvesting in very wet conditions; keep damaged tubers separate.
accepted: fork so the tubers are not cut
harvest sweet potatoes piecemeal as needed
lift Irish potatoes when the leaves turn yellow
avoid harvesting in very wet conditions

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Occupations in Our Community — Crop Growing
questions.q: Give any five ways of storing tuber crops well.
questions.a: Any five of: keep them in a cool, dry, dark, airy place; sort out damaged ones first; store Irish potatoes in crates or on racks, not heaps; dry cassava and make flour; slice and dry sweet potatoes; protect the store from rats and termites.
accepted: protect the store from rats and termites

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Occupations in Our Community — Crop Growing
questions.q: Give any five uses of tuber crops.
questions.a: Any five of: food rich in carbohydrates; income when sold; animal feed from peelings and vines; raw material for flour, starch and chips; planting material for the next season.
accepted: animal feed from peelings and vines
planting material for the next season

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Occupations in Our Community — Crop Growing
questions.q: Which tuber crop grows best in cool areas such as Kabale, and which one resists drought best?
questions.a: Irish potatoes grow best in cool areas such as Kabale; cassava resists drought best.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What are bacteria, and what instrument is used to see them?
questions.a: Bacteria are very tiny living things (micro-organisms) that can only be seen with a microscope.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any five characteristics of bacteria.
questions.a: Any five of: they are very small; they are living and multiply very fast by splitting into two; they have different shapes — round, rod, spiral, comma; most need warmth, moisture, food and darkness; some form spores; some need air and others do not.
accepted: they are living and multiply very fast by splitting into two
some need air and others do not

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Where are bacteria found, and where do they breed best?
questions.a: They are found everywhere — in air, water, soil, food, on the skin and in the body. They breed best in warm, moist, dirty places such as rubbish heaps, stagnant water, uncovered food and dirty latrines.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any five ways in which bacteria are useful.
questions.a: Any five of: making yoghurt, sour milk and cheese; causing decay that returns nutrients to the soil; making manure and compost; fixing nitrogen in legume root nodules; helping digestion in the intestines; making vinegar, medicines and antibiotics; treating sewage; producing biogas.
accepted: causing decay that returns nutrients to the soil
fixing nitrogen in legume root nodules

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any six diseases caused by bacteria and how each is spread.
questions.a: Any six: cholera — dirty water and food; typhoid — contaminated food and water; dysentery — dirty hands and flies; TB — coughing and sneezing; whooping cough and diphtheria — air; tetanus — dirt in wounds; pneumonia — droplets in air.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What are fungi? Give any four examples.
questions.a: Fungi are living things that have no chlorophyll, so they cannot make their own food, and feed on dead or living matter. Examples: mushrooms, yeast, moulds, the ringworm fungus.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any four characteristics of fungi.
questions.a: Any four of: they have no chlorophyll; they have no true roots, stems or leaves; they reproduce by spores; they grow in warm, damp, dark places; some are saprophytes and some parasites.
accepted: some are saprophytes and some parasites

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give the difference between a saprophyte and a parasite.
questions.a: A saprophyte feeds on dead matter, for example the mould on bread; a parasite feeds on a living host, for example the ringworm fungus on human skin.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any four ways in which fungi are useful.
questions.a: Any four of: edible mushrooms as food; yeast for baking and brewing; penicillin and other medicines; causing decay that enriches the soil; flavouring cheese.
accepted: causing decay that enriches the soil

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any four ways in which fungi are harmful.
questions.a: Any four of: they cause human diseases such as ringworm; they cause crop diseases such as blight; they spoil food, leather, clothes and books; some mushrooms are poisonous; moulds produce aflatoxins.
accepted: they cause human diseases such as ringworm
they cause crop diseases such as blight

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name two fungal diseases of human beings and two of crops.
questions.a: Human: ringworm and athlete's foot (also thrush). Crops: potato blight and coffee leaf rust (also maize smut).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What are aflatoxins, and how can they be prevented?
questions.a: Aflatoxins are poisons produced by moulds growing on badly dried food such as groundnuts and maize. They are prevented by drying the produce properly, storing it in a dry, airy place, and throwing away mouldy or discoloured grain.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any eight ways of preventing bacterial and fungal diseases.
questions.a: Any eight of: bathe daily and wash hands with soap; wash, cover and cook food well; boil or treat drinking water; use latrines and dispose of rubbish properly; keep the body and clothes dry; do not share towels, combs or razor blades; sterilise instruments and use antiseptic on wounds; immunise children; take prescribed medicines correctly; dry and store food well.
accepted: bathe daily and wash hands with soap
use latrines and dispose of rubbish properly
keep the body and clothes dry
sterilise instruments and use antiseptic on wounds

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Why should a person finish the full course of antibiotics?
questions.a: Because stopping early leaves some bacteria alive. They then multiply and become resistant, so the same medicine no longer works and the illness returns and is harder to treat.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Why does ironing clothes and drying them in the sun help to prevent skin diseases?
questions.a: Because the fungi and their spores, and parasites such as jiggers and lice, live in damp cloth. The sun's heat and the hot iron kill them, so the clothes are safe to wear.

topics.title: Types of Change — Biological, Physical and Chemical

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Types of Change — Biological, Physical and Chemical
questions.q: What is change? Name the three types.
questions.a: Change is something becoming different from what it was. The three types are biological, physical and chemical.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Types of Change — Biological, Physical and Chemical
questions.q: Name any five agents of change.
questions.a: Any five of: heat and cold, water, air (oxygen and wind), living things such as bacteria, fungi, plants, animals and people, time, chemicals.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Types of Change — Biological, Physical and Chemical
questions.q: What is a biological change? Give any four examples.
questions.a: A biological change is a change that happens in living things as they grow and develop. Examples: germination of a seed; growth of a chick into a hen; a tadpole becoming a frog; decay of dead matter; healing of a wound (any four).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Types of Change — Biological, Physical and Chemical
questions.q: Give the stages of growth in a human being.
questions.a: Baby → child → adolescent → adult → old person.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Types of Change — Biological, Physical and Chemical
questions.q: Give four physical changes that happen to girls and four that happen to boys at adolescence.
questions.a: Girls: breasts develop; hips widen; menstruation begins; pubic and armpit hair grows. Boys: the voice deepens; shoulders broaden; wet dreams begin; pubic, armpit and facial hair grows.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Types of Change — Biological, Physical and Chemical
questions.q: Give any six ways of caring for the body during these changes.
questions.a: Any six of: bathe daily and wash the private parts with clean water; wear clean cotton underwear and change it daily; use and change clean sanitary materials; keep nails short and hair clean; eat well and rest; talk to a trusted adult about worries; choose good friends; abstain from sex.
accepted: bathe daily and wash the private parts with clean water
wear clean cotton underwear and change it daily
use and change clean sanitary materials
keep nails short and hair clean
talk to a trusted adult about worries

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Types of Change — Biological, Physical and Chemical
questions.q: What should a child do if somebody tries to touch his or her private parts?
questions.a: The child should say NO firmly, move away and tell a trusted adult at once — a parent, teacher, health worker, religious leader or the police. It must not be kept secret, and it is never the child's fault.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Types of Change — Biological, Physical and Chemical
questions.q: What is a physical change? Give any five examples.
questions.a: A physical change is one in which no new substance is formed and which can usually be reversed. Examples: melting ice; boiling water; dissolving salt; breaking a stick; bending a wire (any five).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Types of Change — Biological, Physical and Chemical
questions.q: What is a chemical change? Give any five examples.
questions.a: A chemical change is one in which a new substance is formed and which usually cannot be reversed. Examples: burning wood; rusting of iron; cooking food; souring of milk; rotting of fruit (any five).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Types of Change — Biological, Physical and Chemical
questions.q: Give three differences between physical and chemical changes.
questions.a: In a physical change no new substance is formed, it is usually reversible, and only shape, size or state changes; in a chemical change a new substance is formed, it is usually irreversible, and heat, light, gas or a smell is often produced.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Types of Change — Biological, Physical and Chemical
questions.q: Classify each as physical or chemical: melting ice, burning wood, dissolving salt, rusting iron, breaking glass, souring milk.
questions.a: Melting ice — physical; burning wood — chemical; dissolving salt — physical; rusting iron — chemical; breaking glass — physical; souring milk — chemical.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Types of Change — Biological, Physical and Chemical
questions.q: What two things are needed for iron to rust?
questions.a: Air (oxygen) and water (moisture).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Types of Change — Biological, Physical and Chemical
questions.q: Give any four ways of preventing rusting.
questions.a: Any four of: painting; oiling or greasing; galvanising (coating with zinc); coating with plastic; keeping the metal dry; using stainless steel or non-rusting metals.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Types of Change — Biological, Physical and Chemical
questions.q: What is metamorphosis? Give the stages for a butterfly.
questions.a: Metamorphosis is the change of form as an animal grows. For a butterfly: egg → larva (caterpillar) → pupa → adult butterfly.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Types of Change — Biological, Physical and Chemical
questions.q: Why is cooking food said to be a chemical change?
questions.a: Because cooking forms new substances — the food changes in colour, smell, taste and texture, and it cannot be turned back into the raw food it was.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any six external parts of a goat.
questions.a: Any six of: head, horns, beard, eyes, ears, nostrils, mouth, neck, back, udder or scrotum, legs, hooves, tail.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give four differences between a goat and a sheep.
questions.a: A goat has a beard, a tail that points up, a coat of hair, and it browses on leaves; a sheep has no beard, a tail that hangs down, a woolly fleece, and it grazes on grass.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name two local and two exotic breeds of goats.
questions.a: Local: Small East African and Mubende. Exotic: Toggenburg and Saanen (also Alpine, Boer).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name two local and two exotic breeds of sheep.
questions.a: Local: East African Blackhead and Masai. Exotic: Merino and Dorper (also Corriedale).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any five uses of goats and sheep.
questions.a: Any five of: meat; milk; skins and hides; wool from sheep; manure; income and school fees; ceremonies; easy to keep on small land.
accepted: easy to keep on small land

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any six external parts of a pig.
questions.a: Any six of: snout, eyes, ears, bristles, back, hooves (cloven feet), curly tail, udder with teats, flank.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any three exotic breeds of pigs.
questions.a: Any three of: Large White, Landrace, Duroc, Hampshire.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give the meaning of: boar, sow, gilt, farrowing.
questions.a: Boar — a male pig; sow — a female pig that has produced; gilt — a young female pig; farrowing — a pig giving birth.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is the gestation period of a pig?
questions.a: About 114 days — three months, three weeks and three days.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any six qualities of a good house for goats, sheep or pigs.
questions.a: Any six of: raised and well-drained floor; well ventilated but not draughty; strong walls and a leak-proof roof; easy to clean with a slope and drainage; separate pens for the young and the sick; feeding troughs and drinkers; enough space; shade or a wallow for pigs.
accepted: strong walls and a leak-proof roof
easy to clean with a slope and drainage
separate pens for the young and the sick

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Why must a pig house have shade or a wallow?
questions.a: Because pigs cannot sweat, so they cannot cool themselves in the usual way. Shade and a wallow keep them cool and also help control external parasites.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any six ways of managing goats, sheep and pigs well.
questions.a: Any six of: give clean water always; feed a balanced ration with mineral licks; deworm and vaccinate; spray or dip against parasites; clean the house daily; trim hooves; handle them gently; isolate sick animals; keep records; castrate males not needed for breeding.
accepted: feed a balanced ration with mineral licks
castrate males not needed for breeding

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the products got from goats, from sheep and from pigs.
questions.a: Goats: meat, milk, skins, manure, income. Sheep: meat, wool, skins, manure. Pigs: pork, bacon, ham, sausages, lard, bristles, manure.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any four external and any three internal parasites of these animals.
questions.a: External: ticks, lice, mites, fleas (also tsetse flies). Internal: round worms, tape worms, liver flukes (also lung worms).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any five diseases, their signs and how each is prevented or controlled.
questions.a: Any five, for example: pneumonia — coughing and fever, prevented by warm dry housing and treated early; foot and mouth — mouth and hoof sores, controlled by vaccination and quarantine; mange — itching and hair loss, controlled by spraying; worms — thin body and pot belly, controlled by deworming; African swine fever — high fever and sudden death, controlled only by hygiene and quarantine, as there is no cure.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is breastfeeding? For how long should a baby be breastfed exclusively?
questions.a: Breastfeeding is feeding a baby on milk from the mother's breast. A baby should be breastfed exclusively for the first six months, then breastfed with other foods up to two years or beyond.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any four advantages of breastfeeding to the baby and two to the mother.
questions.a: To the baby (any four): breast milk is complete food; colostrum gives antibodies; it is clean, warm and ready; it is easy to digest; it builds love between mother and baby. To the mother: it costs nothing; it helps the womb return to normal (also delays another pregnancy).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is colostrum, and why is it important?
questions.a: Colostrum is the first thick yellow milk produced after birth. It is important because it is rich in antibodies that protect the baby from disease, and in nutrients for a good start.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is bottle feeding? Give two advantages and four disadvantages.
questions.a: Bottle feeding is feeding a baby milk from a bottle. Advantages: anybody can feed the baby; the amount can be measured. Disadvantages: bottles are easily contaminated and cause diarrhoea; formula and bottles are expensive; there are no antibodies; the bond with the mother is weaker; over-dilution causes malnutrition.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: If a mother must bottle feed, what four rules must she follow?
questions.a: Sterilise the bottle and teat by boiling; use boiled water; mix exactly as instructed; feed the milk at once and never keep left-overs (using a cup and spoon is safer).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Who are vulnerable people? Name any five groups.
questions.a: Vulnerable people are those most easily harmed by poor feeding and disease. Any five of: babies and young children; expectant mothers; breastfeeding mothers; the sick, including people with HIV; the elderly; people with disabilities.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What foods does an expectant mother especially need, and why?
questions.a: She needs iron-rich foods (dodo, liver, beans), protein, fruits and vegetables and plenty of water, because she is feeding herself and the growing baby and is at risk of anaemia.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the seven food values and give one example of each.
questions.a: Carbohydrates — matooke; proteins — beans; fats and oils — cooking oil; vitamins — fruits; mineral salts — milk; water — clean drinking water; roughage — vegetables.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is a balanced diet? Give an example of a balanced meal from your home.
questions.a: A balanced diet is a meal containing all the food values in the right amounts. Example: matooke with beans, greens, a fruit and water.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any six deficiency diseases and the food value missing in each.
questions.a: Any six: kwashiorkor — protein; marasmus — energy and protein; anaemia — iron; rickets — vitamin D and calcium; night blindness — vitamin A; scurvy — vitamin C; goitre — iodine; beriberi — vitamin B1.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give the signs of kwashiorkor and of marasmus.
questions.a: Kwashiorkor: swollen legs and face, thin light hair, pot belly, misery and loss of appetite. Marasmus: very thin body, "old man's face", loose skin, ribs showing.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: How can anaemia be prevented?
questions.a: By eating iron-rich foods such as dodo, nakati, liver, beans and meat, together with vitamin C fruits to absorb the iron; by deworming regularly; by sleeping under a treated mosquito net to avoid malaria; and by treating bleeding early.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any six rules of food hygiene.
questions.a: Any six of: wash hands with soap before handling food and eating; wash fruits and vegetables; use clean water and utensils; cover food against flies; keep animals out of the kitchen; do not let a person with diarrhoea or a wound cook for others; wash the cooking place daily.
accepted: wash hands with soap before handling food and eating
keep animals out of the kitchen
do not let a person with diarrhoea

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any four ways of preparing food so that the food value is not lost.
questions.a: Any four of: do not overcook vegetables; steam rather than boil; use the cooking water in the sauce; cut vegetables just before cooking; cook with the lid on; avoid too much oil and salt.
accepted: use the cooking water in the sauce
avoid too much oil and salt

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any five ways of storing food well, and say why mouldy groundnuts must never be eaten.
questions.a: Any five of: dry grains and legumes well; store in clean, dry, airy places; use sacks on pallets or granaries; protect from rats, weevils and moulds; keep milk, meat and cooked food covered and cool and reheat well. Mouldy groundnuts must never be eaten because the moulds produce aflatoxins, poisons that damage the liver and can cause cancer.
accepted: meat and cooked food covered and cool and reheat well. Mouldy groundnuts must never be eaten because the moulds produce aflatoxins
poisons that damage the liver and can cause cancer

topics.title: Primary Health Care and Family Care

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Primary Health Care and Family Care
questions.q: What is Primary Health Care?
questions.a: Primary Health Care is essential health care made available to all people in the community at a cost they can afford, with their full participation, aimed at preventing disease and promoting health.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Primary Health Care and Family Care
questions.q: Name any six elements of PHC.
questions.a: Any six of: health education; proper nutrition; safe water and basic sanitation; maternal and child health including family planning; immunisation; prevention and control of local endemic diseases; treatment of common diseases and injuries; provision of essential drugs; control of HIV/AIDS; care of the disabled and elderly.
accepted: maternal and child health including family planning
prevention and control of local endemic diseases
treatment of common diseases and injuries
care of the disabled and elderly

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Primary Health Care and Family Care
questions.q: Name any four principles of PHC and explain two.
questions.a: Any four of: community participation, equitable distribution, appropriate technology, intersectoral collaboration, focus on prevention, affordability. (Explain two, for example: community participation means the people themselves plan and run their health services; appropriate technology means using simple, cheap methods such as pit latrines and ORS that the community can manage.)
accepted: for example: community participation means the people themselves plan and run their health services
cheap methods such as pit latrines and ORS that the community can manage.)

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Primary Health Care and Family Care
questions.q: Why is prevention said to be better than cure?
questions.a: Because preventing a disease costs far less than treating it, saves lives and suffering, keeps children in school and adults at work, and stops the disease from spreading to others.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Primary Health Care and Family Care
questions.q: Give any six PHC activities that promote community hygiene.
questions.a: Any six of: digging rubbish pits and using latrines; protecting water sources; draining stagnant water and clearing bushes; building drying racks, bath shelters and hand-washing facilities; health education; immunisation days; kitchen gardens; school health clubs and clean-up days.
accepted: digging rubbish pits and using latrines
draining stagnant water and clearing bushes
school health clubs and clean-up days

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Primary Health Care and Family Care
questions.q: Give any five responsibilities of an individual in keeping healthy.
questions.a: Any five of: keep the body clean; eat a balanced diet; use the latrine and wash hands with soap; sleep under a treated net; seek treatment early; avoid alcohol, smoking and drug abuse; keep the surroundings clean.
accepted: use the latrine and wash hands with soap

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Primary Health Care and Family Care
questions.q: Give any five responsibilities of a family in keeping its members healthy.
questions.a: Any five of: build and maintain a latrine, bath shelter, rubbish pit and drying rack; boil or treat drinking water; feed the family well; take children for immunisation; care for the sick, elderly and disabled; keep the home and compound clean.
accepted: keep the home and compound clean

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Primary Health Care and Family Care
questions.q: Give any four responsibilities of the community and four of the government.
questions.a: Community: protect water sources; hold clean-up days; support village health teams; build and maintain health centres (also report outbreaks). Government: train and pay health workers; supply drugs and vaccines; build health centres; make and enforce public health laws (also run health campaigns).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Primary Health Care and Family Care
questions.q: What is a family? Name the four types.
questions.a: A family is a group of people related by blood, marriage or adoption who live together and care for one another. Types: nuclear, extended, single-parent and child-headed.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Primary Health Care and Family Care
questions.q: Give any five duties of parents and five duties of children.
questions.a: Parents: provide food, shelter, clothing, medical care and education; give love, guidance and discipline; protect the children. Children: obey and respect parents; help with chores; go to school and work hard; care for younger ones and the elderly; keep clean; report anything that frightens or hurts them.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Primary Health Care and Family Care
questions.q: How should the family care for a sick person?
questions.a: Give clean bedding and a quiet, airy room; provide soft, tasty food and plenty of fluids; give the medicine on time and complete the dose; keep the person clean and comfortable; watch for danger signs and take them to a health worker quickly.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Primary Health Care and Family Care
questions.q: How should the family care for the elderly and for people with disabilities?
questions.a: The elderly need soft food, warmth, company, help with washing and moving, and respect. People with disabilities need support without pity, help to attend school and work, assistive aids where possible, and full inclusion in family activities.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Primary Health Care and Family Care
questions.q: Name any six things found in a healthy home.
questions.a: Any six of: a clean compound; a latrine; a rubbish pit; a drying rack; a bath shelter; a kitchen with a raised fireplace; clean covered water storage; mosquito nets on the beds; a kitchen garden.
accepted: a kitchen with a raised fireplace

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Primary Health Care and Family Care
questions.q: Who are village health teams, and what do they do?
questions.a: Village health teams are trained community volunteers. They teach families about health, encourage immunisation and use of latrines and nets, treat or refer simple illnesses, follow up sick people and report outbreaks.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Primary Health Care and Family Care
questions.q: Give any four ways in which a school can practise PHC.
questions.a: Any four of: keeping the compound and latrines clean; running hand-washing points with soap; a school health club with drama, posters and talks; growing vegetables in a school garden; inspecting pupils' hygiene; inviting health workers; deworming and immunisation days.
accepted: keeping the compound and latrines clean
a school health club with drama
growing vegetables in a school garden
